note:
v1, THE SKELETON of "Odd Sympathy" (4:53, 108 bpm; Harry, 14 Nov: "okay lets open up one more song in the album. zero's song name choice" / "should skeleton it and then climb both"). The whole shape stands; it is bare.
THE NAME AND THE IDEA: in 1665 Huygens hung two pendulum clocks from one beam and found that however he started them they ended swinging exactly against each other; he called it "an odd kind of sympathy". Common Time keeps one pulse and turns three cells of different lengths under it. This is the other way round: ONE riff, one bar long, on two guitars, left and right, each with its own clock. They start in step. The right guitar's clock runs a hair fast: it slips a sixteenth ahead of the left, holds, slips again, and so on until it is half a bar ahead, exactly against the left. The riff is written so that there, and only there, its two halves fit: every sixteenth of the bar has one guitar on it and never both. A riff with holes becomes a machine with none. The slips are real (the engine's track `warp`, used here for the first time); nothing is shifted by hand.
THE SHAPE: 0:00 the left guitar alone with a pendulum, then bass and kick | 0:18 both guitars in step | 0:53 the first slip (4 bars; the drums thin so it is heard) and a hold a sixteenth apart | 1:11 slip, then an eighth apart | 1:47 three sixteenths | 2:04 a quarter apart | 2:44 the band lets go: two clean guitars tick the riff through a dripping spring, the right one drifting all the way to half a bar; the swarm locks as it arrives | 3:38 AGAINST: the band back, the bar full, the kick on every chug of either guitar | 4:31 the two guitars alone, still against each other; then only the ticks.

Against each other their one line is F F Ab F F F B C, twice a bar: a cell eight sixteenths long, as Common Time's landing riff is. Not planned; it falls out of the riff being its own negative. WHAT IS BARE, on purpose for a skeleton: one riff on one root for the whole piece; no lead, no voice, no second rig (the guitars are Common Time's tight rig, one a side with no doubles); the drum parts are one pattern a section; the drift is 22 bars of the same thing; the five distances between a quarter and a half are passed through, never held.
NOT HEARD BY ANYONE. The slips are the risk: through a high-gain amp a guitar pulling 0 to 139 ms ahead of its twin may read as wide, then flammed, then as a gallop, or just as loose. That is the first thing for an ear.

note:
v2, THE DRIFT GETS A SHAPE (section round: 2:44-3:38, the window the section map called static; v1 had 22 bars of one thing there). The middle of the piece is where the band lets go and the right guitar, now clean, drifts from a quarter of a bar ahead to half a bar. Three things happen under it now.
1. THE GROUND MOVES. A step down every six bars: F, Eb, Db, then C, the dominant, held under the two guitars as they lock against each other, so the lock arrives unresolved and the band's return on F (3:38) is the resolution.
2. THE PENDULUM LETS GO TOO. From 2:58 its tick-tock speeds up for ever and is never faster (a Risset rhythm: the engine's track `risset`, used in a song for the first time). Every fourth bar the tick is back on the bar line at the speed it started. Where the guitars lock (3:33) the plain pendulum has it again. So the drift holds three clocks: the left guitar on the grid, the right one 1% fast, the pendulum for ever accelerating; then one.
3. THE LAST SIX BARS BUILD: the bass on the dominant, the kick on one and three, floor tom into the fill.

v3, THE TWINS (palette round: the guitars, everywhere). Until now Odd Sympathy played on Common Time's tight rig, a different amp each side, with a plate reverb on each guitar. Two things were wrong with that for this piece. It is one riff on two clocks, so the two guitars should be one guitar twice. And it is about what fills the riff's rests, so a rest has to be silence; the plate filled them. Both guitars now play one new library patch, ct-twin: the same string and pick into the engine's `modern` amp and the engine's own cabinet, then a gate and nothing after it. Each side has its own speaker cone, and the two share one small room on their bus: the beam the two clocks hang from.

note:
v4, THE HOLD AN EIGHTH APART GETS ITS OWN GROUND AND ITS OWN BEAT (section round: 1:20-1:47, the window the section map called static). Until now every hold was the same riff on F with a different kick. An eighth apart the canon does something no other distance does: the right guitar plays each hook note and the left answers it an eighth later. So this hold is now built on the eighth, three ways.
1. THE GROUND MOVES, for the first time under the heavy guitars: the riff goes up to Ab, the hook's minor third. The right guitar, being ahead, gets there an eighth before the bar line. (The plan for the next rounds: the holds take the hook's own notes as their grounds, Ab, then B, then C.)
2. THE BEAT: the hi-hat in eighths, a china on the bar line, and the snare answering itself, a ghost stroke an eighth after each backbeat, as each hook note is answered.
3. THE BASS plays both guitars' notes there: the one line the two make at this distance.

note:
v5, TWO VOICES, and the kit's top falls as the records' does (whole-song round). The piece had no voice and no tune: a riff and its canon. It now has the same idea in speech. Two voices, left and right, twins like the guitars, say the same four lines, a syllable to each attack of the riff; the right voice is on the right guitar's clock, so it slips with it and nothing is placed by hand.
   I cannot hear you through the wall / only the floor between us moves / whatever way you lean I lean / against you until we agree
(Two clocks on one beam, from the inside.) The lines are heard three ways, as the riff is:
- 0:36, IN STEP: the four lines spoken, the two voices together, a line every two bars.
- 2:13, A QUARTER APART: the four lines spoken again, the right voice a beat ahead of the left, so every syllable is said twice.
- 3:46, 4:04, 4:22, AGAINST: the last line only, barked, four times round each time: half a bar apart the two voices' syllables interlock as the guitars' notes do.
Spoken first and barked last because a speech recogniser, on the voice alone, reads 18 of the 24 words spoken on this rhythm and far fewer barked.

note:
v6, THE HOLD THREE SIXTEENTHS APART IS BUILT ON THE HITS (section round: 1:47-2:04 and the slip into it; the section map's window 1:46-2:22, "little new"). Each hold is now getting what only its distance has. An eighth apart it was the echo (v4). Three sixteenths apart the two guitars strike TOGETHER five times a bar, more than at any other distance, and three of those five are two different notes: the riff makes chords with itself (a tritone, a minor third, a fifth). So:
1. THE BAND STOPS KEEPING TIME there and strikes only where the two guitars strike together: kick on all five, snare on two of the chords, a china on the bar line, the bass on the five and resting between. The two dry guitars carry the whole riff through the gaps; the pendulum from the opening ticks under them.
2. THE GROUND MOVES AGAIN, to B, the hook's tritone, from the slip at 1:47. The hook's notes are becoming the song's grounds one by one: Ab at an eighth, B here. The quarter hold after it is back on F for now.

note:
v7, THE WORDS ARE HEARD (whole-song round). chirp-eco read v5's spoken lines with a speech recogniser IN THE MIX and found the band covered them: 5 words of 24, and each voice 2 to 3 dB under the quietest voice on eleven records. Four changes, all to the two spoken passages (0:36 and 2:13):
1. IN STEP THERE IS ONE VOICE, in the middle. Two copies of one voice in unison smeared each other, and it is the idea anyway: when the two clocks agree there is one voice. It splits in two only when they part.
2. A BEAT APART (2:13) the two voices now stand wide, left and right, so each ear has its own.
3. THE VOICE IS RE-VOICED. Measured alone it was a dull voice: most of its energy under 1 kHz and little at 1-4 kHz, where words are told apart and the guitars are loudest. Its body is cut and its middle lifted.
4. THE GUITARS BREATHE WITH THE SPEECH: they fall 5 dB under each syllable (a pump keyed from the voice's notes; the album's first use of it) and come back between lines.
Also the kit's top filter moves to Common Time's fit.

v8, THE HOLD A SIXTEENTH APART: EVERY SIXTEENTH STRUCK, ON C (section round: 1:02-1:11; the section map's window 0:35-1:11, "little new"). This was the one hold with nothing of its own. A sixteenth apart is as close as the two guitars come without being together: every note has a shadow a sixteenth before it, and between them they strike thirteen of the bar's sixteen sixteenths. So:
1. THE BAND PLAYS EVERYTHING EITHER GUITAR PLAYS: the kick and the bass on all thirteen. The drummer fills the three sixteenths that are left (a tom, the floor tom, the snare). For four bars every sixteenth of the bar is struck: the densest passage before the end.
2. IT STANDS ON C, the hook's third note. All three of the hook's notes are now grounds, one for each odd distance: C a sixteenth apart, Ab an eighth apart, B three sixteenths apart. The song's three simple distances (together, a beat apart, half a bar apart) stay on F and carry the words.
The three odd distances now each show one thing: a sixteenth apart everything either guitar plays; an eighth apart the echo; three sixteenths apart only what they play together.
